article.title: Fitzpatrick Skin Type Test: 5-Question Quiz and Results
article.meta_description: Take a quick Fitzpatrick skin type test, see what types I to VI mean, and learn how it differs from skin tone and undertone for makeup and style.
article.h1: Fitzpatrick Skin Type Test: A 5-Question Self-Quiz (Types I to VI)
article.body_html:
A Fitzpatrick skin type test sorts you into one of six types, I to VI, based on how your skin usually reacts to sun: whether it burns, whether it tans, and how deeply. The quick quiz below gives you a rough self-estimate in about two minutes. It is a general guide, not a clinical result, and it is a different thing from your skin tone or undertone.

Fitzpatrick skin type test: the short answer

What the scale is

The Fitzpatrick scale was developed by dermatologist Thomas Fitzpatrick in the 1970s to describe how different skin responds to ultraviolet light. Type I is skin that burns very easily and barely tans. Type VI is deeply pigmented skin that very rarely burns. Types II to V sit in between.

What this quiz can and can't tell you

It can give you a reasonable starting estimate of your sun reactivity, and it can clear up the confusion between sun reaction, skin depth and undertone. It can't classify your skin clinically, assess your health, or tell you anything about a specific spot or mark. For that, you need a professional.

What the Fitzpatrick scale measures (and what it doesn't)

Sun reaction: burning and tanning tendency

Everything on the scale comes back to two questions: how readily do you burn, and how readily do you tan? That is why the questions below focus on past sun reactions rather than appearance alone.

Why it isn't a measure of how light or dark skin looks

Two people can look similar in photos and react to sun differently. Two people with different looks can fall in the same type. Pigment and reaction tend to travel together, which is why color questions appear in quizzes, but they are only clues.

Why it isn't a health assessment

Your type describes a general tendency. It does not tell you whether a mole, patch or change in your skin is a concern.

Before you start: how to answer fairly

  • Think about your usual reaction, not your best tan. Recall what typically happens at the start of a season, not the result after weeks of gradual exposure.
  • Ignore sunscreen, recent tans and one-off burns. A single bad burn on a cloudy day with no protection doesn't define you. Look for the pattern.
  • Answer about your natural coloring. Skip dyed hair and colored contact lenses.

If you can't remember how your skin reacts, choose the option that fits your family pattern and the way you've seen your skin respond over several years.

The self-test: 5 questions

Score each answer from 0 to 4. Write down your five numbers and add them up at the end.

Question 1: What is your natural skin color in areas rarely exposed to sun?

  • 0: Very pale or ivory
  • 1: Fair or light beige
  • 2: Medium beige or light olive
  • 3: Olive or light-to-medium brown
  • 4: Deep brown to very deep brown

Question 2: What are your natural eye and hair colors?

  • 0: Red or very light blond hair, light blue, green or gray eyes
  • 1: Blond or light brown hair, blue, green or hazel eyes
  • 2: Medium brown hair, light brown or hazel eyes
  • 3: Dark brown hair, brown eyes
  • 4: Black or near-black hair, very dark brown eyes

Question 3: What usually happens after your first unprotected sun exposure of a season?

  • 0: A painful burn, often with blistering or peeling
  • 1: A burn, usually followed by peeling
  • 2: A mild burn, sometimes
  • 3: I rarely burn
  • 4: I almost never burn

Question 4: Does your skin tan afterward, and how deeply?

  • 0: Never. I turn red, then back to my usual color, and may freckle
  • 1: A faint tan, with difficulty
  • 2: A gradual light-to-medium tan
  • 3: I tan easily to a moderate brown
  • 4: I tan deeply and quickly, or my skin is already deeply pigmented with little visible change

Question 5: How does your face react to sun compared with the rest of your body?

  • 0: My face reddens very quickly
  • 1: My face reddens fairly easily
  • 2: My face sometimes reddens
  • 3: My face rarely reddens
  • 4: I hardly ever notice a reaction on my face

How to add up your answers

Total scoreApproximate type
0 to 3Type I
4 to 7Type II
8 to 11Type III
12 to 15Type IV
16 to 18Type V
19 to 20Type VI

These ranges are a simplified way to organize your answers. Treat the result as a ballpark. If questions 3 and 4 (burning and tanning) point to a different type than questions 1 and 2 (coloring), give more weight to 3 and 4, because the scale is about reaction.

Your result: Fitzpatrick types I to VI at a glance

Types I and II: burn easily, tan little

Type I typically burns every time and doesn't tan. Type II burns easily and tans minimally. Both are often associated with very fair skin and light eyes or hair, though not always.

Types III and IV: sometimes burn, tan gradually

Type III may burn at first, then tans to a light brown. Type IV burns only a little and tans readily to a moderate brown. These two types cover a wide range of looks, including many medium and olive complexions.

Types V and VI: rarely burn, tan deeply or have deeply pigmented skin

Type V rarely burns and tans darkly. Type VI very rarely burns and has deeply pigmented skin. Burning is less common but still possible, so sun protection still matters.

If you land between two types

That is normal. Many people sit on the border, such as II/III or IV/V. Note both and don't force a single answer. A borderline result is a good reason to rely on a professional if the type actually matters for a decision.

Why a self-test can be off

Memory, past tans and sunscreen habits skew answers

If you always wear sunscreen, you may never have seen your skin's unprotected reaction. If you've tanned for years, your recent history may not reflect your natural response.

Why the scale can feel too broad for deeper skin tones

Many people with deeper skin feel the scale lumps them into two types, V and VI, despite a wide range of depth and undertone. That criticism is fair. The scale was built around sun reaction, not to describe the full variety of skin color.

Why a quiz is a rough guide and not a clinical classification

A professional can consider your history, your family background and your skin directly. A five-question quiz can't, so use it as an estimate.

Fitzpatrick type vs skin tone vs undertone

Three different questions

  • Fitzpatrick type: how your skin reacts to sun.
  • Skin depth (tone): how light or deep your skin looks.
  • Undertone: the cool, warm, neutral or olive cast beneath the surface.

Why the same type can need different foundation shades

Two people who are both Type III could be a light neutral and a medium warm in foundation terms. The scale says nothing about depth or undertone, so it can't pick a shade for you.

Which to use for what

For makeup shades and clothing colors, depth and undertone are the useful measures. Our guide to finding your depth and undertone walks through it, and the undertone tests are a quick way to check the cool-versus-warm question.

Sun safety and skin health: not medical advice

Every type needs sun protection

A higher number doesn't mean you can skip sunscreen, shade or protective clothing. Skin of every type can be affected by sun exposure.

Your type doesn't tell you about a spot or mole

Your Fitzpatrick type can't tell you whether a mole, patch or change in your skin is a concern.

When to see a dermatologist or doctor

This article and any AI feedback are not medical advice, so please see a dermatologist or doctor for any skin concern, and for decisions about laser treatments or tanning, where settings should be assessed by a professional.

Using your results for style and makeup

Skip Fitzpatrick for shade matching

Use the quiz to understand your sun reactivity, then put it aside for beauty decisions. Foundation, blush and clothing colors depend on depth and undertone.

Simple starting points once you know your tone

  • Cool undertone: try berry or rosy lip colors, and clothing in navy, emerald, or cool gray. For example, a navy blazer with a white tee and gray trousers.
  • Warm undertone: try peach or terracotta blush, and clothing in olive, camel, or rust. For example, an olive overshirt over a cream tee with tan chinos.
  • Neutral or olive undertone: you can often wear both families. Test by holding a fabric near your face in daylight and seeing whether your skin looks fresh or dull.

For makeup choices based on your features, the makeup self-quiz is a good next step.

Where FitCheck AI can fit in (and where it can't)

What the live skin analysis gives you

FitCheck AI's live skin analysis uses the camera to give an AI skin overview with cosmetic beauty suggestions. It's a second opinion on the style side, not a measurement.

What it doesn't do

It does not assign a Fitzpatrick type, and it does not assess skin health or detect or treat any skin condition. Its feedback is an AI opinion and a starting point, and it is not medical advice.

Photo tips

For the best result, face natural light, hold the camera at eye level and avoid filters. Filters and warm indoor bulbs can change how your skin color appears.

faqs.question: Can my Fitzpatrick type change over time?
faqs.answer: The type describes your skin's typical tendency, and it is generally treated as stable. Your actual coloring can look different with a seasonal tan or a lot of sun, but that doesn't usually mean you've changed type. If you're unsure, a dermatologist can assess it.

faqs.question: Is Fitzpatrick type the same as skin tone?
faqs.answer: No. Fitzpatrick type is about how your skin reacts to sun, while skin tone describes how light or deep your skin looks, and undertone describes its cool, warm or neutral cast. They tend to overlap, but they answer different questions.

faqs.question: Can I use my Fitzpatrick type to choose foundation?
faqs.answer: Not reliably. People of the same type can need very different shades because depth and undertone vary within each type. Use swatches in natural daylight along jaw and neck instead.

faqs.question: Does a higher number mean I don't need sunscreen?
faqs.answer: No. Types V and VI burn less often, but sun protection still matters for every type. A dermatologist or doctor can advise on sun care for your situation.

faqs.question: Can an app tell me my Fitzpatrick type?
faqs.answer: FitCheck AI does not assign a Fitzpatrick type. Its live skin analysis offers a cosmetic AI overview and beauty suggestions, not a medical or clinical classification.

review.notes: The article delivers what the query asks for: a working 5-question quiz with scoring, a type I-VI explanation, limitations, the difference between Fitzpatrick type, skin tone and undertone, and sun-safety referrals. The scale background is accurate (Thomas Fitzpatrick, 1970s, sun reaction rather than appearance). The descriptions of types I-VI are consistent with standard definitions. App claims stay within APP_FACTS: live skin analysis is described as a cosmetic AI overview, not medical, with no Fitzpatrick typing, no accuracy numbers, no storage or privacy claims, and Android only. Nothing is invented (no stats, studies or testimonials). Minor suggestions: (1) The 0-20 scoring bands are the author's own simplification, not the validated 10-item Fitzpatrick questionnaire. The text already calls it 'approximate' and 'simplified'; adding one line that it is not the clinical questionnaire would make this clearer. (2) Q1 and Q2 (coloring) carry the same weight as the reaction questions in the total, even though the text then says to prioritize Q3 and Q4. Consider weighting them or reordering. (3) Confirm that the internal links (/ai-skin-analysis/, /blog/what-is-my-skin-tone/, and the others) resolve. (4) The tone is somewhat repetitive: 'not medical advice' and 'rough guide' appear many times. Trimming would improve readability.
